task_row_model.query: In a 58-year-old with progressive exertional dyspnea, new atrial fibrillation, elevated NT-proBNP, preserved LVEF (60%) and increased left ventricular wall thickness on echocardiogram, what clinical features and diagnostic tests best distinguish hypertensive concentric remodeling causing HFpEF from restrictive cardiomyopathy due to cardiac amyloidosis? What is the recommended diagnostic sequence?

documents.content: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is commonly associated with long-standing hypertension and concentric left ventricular remodeling. Echocardiography typically shows preserved LVEF, increased relative wall thickness, left atrial enlargement and diastolic dysfunction with impaired relaxation and elevated filling pressures; measures such as E/e' ratio, LA volume index and pulmonary venous Doppler are useful. Initial evaluation includes ECG, natriuretic peptide testing and assessment of comorbidities (hypertension, obesity, diabetes). Management focuses on blood pressure control, diuretics for congestion and treating comorbid conditions; advanced imaging is used when atypical features appear.

Distinguishing hypertensive concentric remodeling from cardiac amyloidosis requires correlation of clinical, ECG, echocardiographic and laboratory/imaging findings. Key red flags for amyloid: disproportionate increase in wall thickness with low-voltage ECG, unexplained orthostatic hypotension, neuropathy, and rapidly progressive heart failure. Echocardiography may show restrictive filling, biatrial enlargement, and speckled myocardium; strain imaging frequently demonstrates apical sparing. Recommended sequence: ECG and focused echo plus strain, serum and urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation and serum free light chains to screen for AL amyloidosis, then bone-avid transthyretin scintigraphy (99mTc-PYP/DPD/HMDP) to detect ATTR. Cardiac MRI with LGE and T1 mapping helps when noninvasive tests are inconclusive. Endomyocardial biopsy remains the gold standard if diagnoses conflict.

Cardiac amyloidosis is caused by extracellular deposition of misfolded proteins, most commonly transthyretin (ATTR) or immunoglobulin light chains (AL). Clinical presentation includes progressive exertional intolerance, signs of right-sided congestion, and conduction disease. Diagnostic tools include serum and urine studies to detect monoclonal proteins for AL, bone scintigraphy (technetium-labeled PYP/DPD/HMDP) that can identify ATTR, and confirmatory endomyocardial biopsy with Congo red staining and typing. Management differs by subtype: AL requires chemotherapy targeted at the plasma cell clone; ATTR may be treated with TTR-stabilizing or TTR-silencing agents and symptomatic care for heart failure.

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is characterized by unexplained myocardial hypertrophy, often asymmetric and involving the interventricular septum. Patients may present with exertional dyspnea, syncope, or palpitations; a systolic ejection murmur and dynamic outflow obstruction may be present. Diagnosis relies on echocardiography demonstrating asymmetric septal hypertrophy, systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve and provokable gradients; cardiac MRI refines morphological assessment and fibrosis with late gadolinium enhancement. Genetic testing and family screening are integral because HCM is commonly inherited, and management includes beta-blockers, disopyramide, septal reduction therapies, and ICD consideration for sudden death risk.

Chronic lung disease and interstitial lung disease produce progressive dyspnea and can elevate natriuretic peptides when associated with right ventricular strain or pulmonary hypertension. Pulmonary function testing, high-resolution CT of the chest, arterial blood gas analysis and six-minute walk testing help determine parenchymal versus vascular causes. Treatment targets the underlying pulmonary condition and oxygenation; cardiology evaluation is indicated when cardiac comorbidity is suspected, but preserved left ventricular systolic function on echocardiography usually points away from primary left-sided cardiomyopathy.
